raw_text:
**Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review**

The clinical progression of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has undergone transformative iterations. Early balloon angioplasty was limited by acute recoil and vessel remodeling, leading to the introduction of bare-metal stents (BMS) [1]. While BMS addressed acute vascular closure, in-stent restenosis remained a significant challenge. The subsequent advent of drug-eluting stents (DES) drastically reduced restenosis by eluting antiproliferative agents from durable polymers [2]. However, modern permanent metallic stents leave a rigid cage predisposing the patient to long-term risks such as very late stent thrombosis, chronic vascular inflammation, and the "jailing" of side branches. These limitations catalyzed the concept of "vascular restoration therapy," utilizing bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) [3,4], promising transient mechanical support followed by complete resorption to restore vasomotion [5].

The first commercially successful platform was the polymeric poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA)-based Absorb everolimus-eluting BVS (Abbott Vascular) [6]. Initial feasibility studies, such as the ABSORB Cohort A and B trials, demonstrated successful scaffold resorption and restored vasomotion [7]. Encouraged by these results, massive randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluated BVS against metallic everolimus-eluting stents (EES). Unfortunately, these trials revealed significant safety concerns. The ABSORB II [8], ABSORB III [9], and ABSORB IV [10] trials, alongside the routine-clinical-use AIDA trial [11], consistently demonstrated that the first-generation Absorb BVS was associated with higher rates of target lesion failure (TLF) and an elevated risk of scaffold thrombosis (ST). Long-term five-year data from the ABSORB III trial confirmed that safety events continued to accumulate until complete bioresorption was achieved [12]. Subsequent large-scale meta-analyses corroborated these findings, reporting a two- to three-fold higher rate of early, late, and very late scaffold thrombosis compared to metallic EES [13,14,15].

The mechanical and biological mechanisms driving first-generation BVS failure were clarified through intracoronary imaging registries like the INVEST study [16,17]. First, PLLA has lower tensile strength than cobalt-chromium. To achieve equivalent radial strength, the Absorb BVS required a strut thickness of 150 µm (compared to ~60–80 µm for modern metallic DES). These thick struts disrupted laminar flow, caused local shear stress disturbances, and delayed endothelialization. Second, suboptimal deployment—marked by scaffold underexpansion, malapposition, and late structural dismantling—created a pro-thrombotic milieu [18]. 

To mitigate these mechanical pitfalls, investigators formulated a standardized implantation protocol known as the "PSP" technique: meticulous Pre-dilatation with non-compliant balloons, precise vessel Sizing (restricting use to vessels with a reference diameter ≥2.25 mm), and mandatory high-pressure Post-dilatation [18,19]. Clinical registries validated that strictly adhering to the PSP protocol significantly reduced TLF and ST rates [20,21].

Driven by these insights, next-generation BVS have been engineered using advanced polymeric materials or biocorrodible alloys to optimize strut thickness and vascular healing. Polymeric advancements include the tyrosine-polycarbonate-based Fantom scaffold (REVA Medical). In the FANTOM II trial, its 125 µm radiopaque struts showed highly favorable vascular healing and five-year safety outcomes [22]. Similarly, the 100–125 µm PLLA-based Firesorb scaffold demonstrated excellent tissue coverage and minimal late lumen loss in the FUTURE-II trial, with zero reported scaffold thromboses [23]. Furthermore, the MeRes-1 trial validated the MeRes100 platform, a 100 µm PLLA BVS, yielding a 1.87% MACE rate at three years with no thrombotic events [24]. 

Biocorrodible metallic alloys represent another major breakthrough. The sirolimus-eluting magnesium-based Magmaris (DREAMS 2G) scaffold possesses 150 µm struts but undergoes much faster resorption (~12 months) compared to PLLA (~3 years). The safety of this platform was established in the BIOSOLVE-II trial [25] and subsequently confirmed in the real-world BIOSOLVE-IV registry [26]. However, the MAGSTEMI randomized trial in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) patients reported higher late lumen loss and a lower rate of complete vascular healing for Magmaris compared to metallic DES, emphasizing the need for selective lesion application [27]. More recently, biocorrodible iron-based scaffolds (IBS) have emerged. Utilizing nitrided pure iron, IBS can achieve ultra-thin profiles (53–70 µm) while preserving high radial strength. Long-term preclinical evaluations in porcine models by Zheng et al. demonstrated high biocompatibility, excellent endothelialization, and a controlled degradation profile without toxicity [28].

Currently, clinical guidelines do not recommend the routine use of first-generation polymeric BVS [21]. However, the paradigm of "leaving nothing behind" remains highly attractive. As highlighted by Stone et al. [29], bioresorbable scaffolds are poised for a substantial clinical resurgence. Next-generation designs featuring ultra-thin struts (<100 µm), faster degradation times, and advanced biocorrodible alloys, when guided systematically by intravascular imaging and strict PSP protocols, offer a powerful, long-term therapeutic option for coronary artery disease [30].
